notes.h: Key ideas and curved arrows (Higher Level only)
points: A reaction mechanism is the step-by-step description of how a reaction happens: which bonds break, which form, and how the electrons move.
Homolytic fission: a covalent bond breaks so that each atom keeps one of the two bonding electrons, forming two free radicals, e.g. Cl–Cl → Cl• + Cl•.
Heterolytic fission: a covalent bond breaks so that one atom takes both bonding electrons, forming a positive and a negative ion, e.g. Cl–Cl → Cl⁺ + Cl⁻.
A free radical is an atom or group of atoms with an unpaired electron, shown by a dot, e.g. Cl• or •CH₃; free radicals are very reactive and short-lived.
A curved arrow with a full arrowhead shows the movement of a pair of electrons, drawn from where the pair starts (a bond or a lone pair) to where it ends up.
A fishhook arrow, with a half arrowhead, shows the movement of a single electron; two fishhooks from one bond show homolytic fission.
A carbocation (carbonium ion) is an ion with a positive charge on a carbon atom, e.g. CH₃CH₂⁺ or CH₂ClCH₂⁺.
A chain reaction is one in which a product of one step is a reactant in another step, so the reaction keeps itself going.

notes.h: Free radical substitution of methane (Higher Level only)
points: Overall: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, in ultraviolet light (monochlorination).
Initiation: UV light causes homolytic fission of chlorine molecules, Cl₂ → 2Cl•; draw two fishhooks from the Cl–Cl bond, one to each chlorine atom.
Propagation step 1: a chlorine radical takes a hydrogen atom from methane, Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃, forming a methyl radical.
Propagation step 2: the methyl radical takes a chlorine atom from a chlorine molecule, •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•.
The Cl• formed in step 2 starts step 1 again, so the two propagation steps form a chain reaction.
Termination: two radicals combine, removing radicals and ending a chain: Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂; •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl; •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆ (ethane).
With more chlorine, further substitution gives dichloromethane, trichloromethane and tetrachloromethane, so a mixture of products is formed.

notes.h: Free radical substitution of ethane (Higher Level only)
points: Overall: C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl, giving chloroethane, in ultraviolet light.
Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl•.
Propagation: Cl• + C₂H₆ → HCl + •C₂H₅, forming an ethyl radical; then •C₂H₅ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + Cl•.
Termination: Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂; •C₂H₅ + Cl• → C₂H₅Cl; •C₂H₅ + •C₂H₅ → C₄H₁₀ (butane).

notes.h: Evidence for the free radical mechanism (Higher Level only)
points: The reaction does not happen in the dark at room temperature but starts in UV light, which supplies the energy to split Cl₂ into radicals in initiation.
Thousands of molecules of product form for every photon of light absorbed, because one radical starts a long chain of propagation steps.

Traces of ethane form in the chlorination of methane, and traces of butane in the chlorination of ethane; these can only come from two methyl or two ethyl radicals joining in termination, so the radicals must exist.

Termination is rare, because radicals are present at very low concentration; a radical is far more likely to collide with a CH₄ or Cl₂ molecule than with another radical, so the ethane or butane is only a trace.
Adding a substance that produces free radicals, such as tetramethyl lead, Pb(CH₃)₄, speeds up the reaction, which shows that radicals are involved.
Adding oxygen, which combines with free radicals, slows the reaction, which shows that a radical chain is being broken.

notes.h: Ionic addition of chlorine to ethene (Higher Level only)
points: Overall: CH₂=CH₂ + Cl₂ → CH₂ClCH₂Cl, giving 1,2-dichloroethane.

Step 1, polarisation: the C=C double bond is a region of high electron density from its pi electrons; as a Cl₂ molecule approaches, these electrons repel the electrons of the Cl–Cl bond, inducing a dipole Clδ⁺–Clδ⁻.
Step 2, heterolytic fission: the Cl–Cl bond breaks with both electrons going to the further chlorine atom, giving Cl⁺ and Cl⁻; draw a curved arrow from the Cl–Cl bond to the Clδ⁻ atom.

Step 3, carbocation formation: the pair of pi electrons forms a bond to Cl⁺, so one carbon bonds to Cl while the other, having lost its share of the pi pair, carries a positive charge, giving CH₂ClCH₂⁺; draw a curved arrow from the C=C pi bond to Cl⁺.
Step 4, attack by the negative ion: Cl⁻ uses a lone pair to bond to the positive carbon, giving 1,2-dichloroethane; draw a curved arrow from a lone pair on Cl⁻ to the C⁺.
It is called ionic addition because the two parts add as ions, one after the other.

notes.h: Ionic addition of hydrogen chloride to ethene (Higher Level only)
points: Overall: CH₂=CH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂Cl, giving chloroethane.
The H–Cl bond is already polar, Hδ⁺–Clδ⁻, because chlorine is more electronegative, so no dipole needs to be induced.

Step 1: the pi electrons of C=C form a bond to the Hδ⁺ atom, and the H–Cl bond breaks heterolytically, giving Cl⁻ and the carbocation CH₃CH₂⁺; draw a curved arrow from the pi bond to H, and one from the H–Cl bond to Cl.
Step 2: Cl⁻ bonds to the positive carbon, giving chloroethane; draw a curved arrow from a lone pair on Cl⁻ to C⁺.
Evidence that the H–X bond breaks in the mechanism: the rate of addition to ethene increases in the order HF < HCl < HBr < HI, the order in which the H–X bond gets weaker.

notes.h: Evidence for the ionic addition mechanism (Higher Level only)
points: When ethene reacts with chlorine water, the products include 2-chloroethanol, CH₂ClCH₂OH, as well as 1,2-dichloroethane.
2-chloroethanol forms because a water molecule, using a lone pair on its oxygen, attacks the carbocation instead of Cl⁻, and then loses H⁺.
This shows the reaction happens in steps through a positively charged intermediate: if both chlorine atoms added at the same moment, no 2-chloroethanol could form.
With bromine water containing sodium chloride, ethene gives 1-bromo-2-chloroethane, CH₂BrCH₂Cl, as well as 1,2-dibromoethane.
The Cl⁻ ions attack the carbocation, but no 1,2-dichloroethane forms, because the first atom to add is always from Br₂.

notes.h: Comparing the two mechanisms (Higher Level only)
points: Free radical substitution is shown by alkanes, involves homolytic fission, needs UV light, has radical intermediates and uses fishhook arrows.
Ionic addition is shown by alkenes, involves heterolytic fission, needs no light, has a carbocation intermediate and uses curved arrows.
Diagram: the four steps of ionic addition of Cl₂ to ethene, with the δ⁺ and δ⁻ charges, the carbocation and every curved arrow, and the initiation step of chlorination with its two fishhooks.

keyTerms.definition: A step-by-step description of how a reaction happens, showing which bonds break and form and how the electrons move.
The breaking of a covalent bond so that each atom takes one of the bonding electrons, forming free radicals.
The breaking of a covalent bond so that one atom takes both bonding electrons, forming ions.
An atom or group of atoms with an unpaired electron, which is very reactive.
An arrow with a full arrowhead, showing the movement of a pair of electrons in a mechanism.
An arrow with a half arrowhead, showing the movement of a single electron in a mechanism.
An ion with a positive charge on a carbon atom, formed as an intermediate in ionic addition.
A reaction in which a product of one step is a reactant in the next, so the reaction is self-sustaining.
The first step of a radical chain reaction, in which radicals are first formed, usually by UV light.
The steps of a radical chain reaction in which a radical reacts and a new radical is formed.
The step of a radical chain reaction in which two radicals combine and the chain ends.

questions.prompt: Describe the mechanism of the reaction between ethane and chlorine in ultraviolet light to form chloroethane. State two pieces of evidence for the mechanism and explain how each supports it.
questions.model: Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl•, drawn with two fishhooks from the Cl–Cl bond. Propagation: Cl• + C₂H₆ → HCl + •C₂H₅, then •C₂H₅ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + Cl•; the Cl• regenerated starts the next propagation step, so the steps form a chain. Termination: Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂; •C₂H₅ + Cl• → C₂H₅Cl; •C₂H₅ + •C₂H₅ → C₄H₁₀. Evidence 1: the reaction does not occur in the dark at room temperature but starts in UV light, which supplies the energy to split Cl₂ into radicals. Evidence 2: thousands of molecules of product form for each photon absorbed, which shows a chain reaction in which one radical starts many propagation steps. Evidence 3, if a third is given: traces of butane form, which can only come from two ethyl radicals joining, so the radicals must exist; the butane is only a trace because termination is rare, since radicals are at very low concentration and mostly collide with C₂H₆ or Cl₂ molecules.

questions.prompt: Describe, using curved arrows, the mechanism of the addition of chlorine to ethene. Explain how the formation of 2-chloroethanol when ethene reacts with chlorine water supports this mechanism.
questions.model: Step 1: the pi electrons of the C=C bond repel the electrons of the Cl–Cl bond, polarising it to Clδ⁺–Clδ⁻. Step 2: a curved arrow from the Cl–Cl bond to the Clδ⁻ atom shows heterolytic fission, giving Cl⁺ and Cl⁻. Step 3: a curved arrow from the C=C pi bond to Cl⁺ forms a C–Cl bond, leaving a carbocation, CH₂ClCH₂⁺. Step 4: a curved arrow from a lone pair on Cl⁻ to the positive carbon forms 1,2-dichloroethane. In chlorine water, a water molecule can attack the carbocation instead of Cl⁻, giving 2-chloroethanol, CH₂ClCH₂OH, after loss of H⁺. Because 2-chloroethanol forms, the reaction must proceed through a positively charged carbocation intermediate: if both chlorine atoms added at the same moment, no 2-chloroethanol could be formed.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between homolytic and heterolytic fission, giving an example of each from the reactions of chlorine.
questions.model: Homolytic fission is the breaking of a covalent bond so that each atom keeps one of the two bonding electrons, forming two free radicals. Example: in the initiation step of chlorination, Cl–Cl → Cl• + Cl•, drawn with two fishhooks. Heterolytic fission is the breaking of a covalent bond so that one atom takes both bonding electrons, forming a positive and a negative ion. Example: in the addition of chlorine to ethene, Cl–Cl → Cl⁺ + Cl⁻, drawn with a curved arrow.
